specPoints.text: understand the mechanisms of the nucleophilic substitution reactions between primary halogenoalkanes and: i aqueous potassium hydroxide ii ammonia S N 1 and S N 2 substitution mechanisms will be tested in Unit 4.

primer.text: Watch the electrons: the nucleophile's lone pair lands on the d+ carbon while the bonding pair escapes with the halide. This note draws the hydroxide mechanism in one concerted step and the ammonia mechanism in two, right through to the neutral amine and its ammonium co-product.

lessons.title: The polarised C-X bond sets the stage
lessons.opening: A nucleophilic substitution is a takeover at the carbon atom: the nucleophile attacks the d+ carbon, and the d- halogen departs with its electron pair. Halogenoalkanes invite this chemistry precisely because the C-X bond is polar.
keyPoints: A nucleophilic substitution involves a nucleophile attacking a carbon atom carrying a partial positive charge.
The atom carrying a partial negative charge (the halogen) is replaced by the nucleophile.
Halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution due to the polar C-X bond.
Electronegativity differences make carbon d+ and halogen d-, opening the door for electron-pair donation.

low.restatement: Electronegativity splits the bond: carbon holds the d+ badge, halogen the d- badge; the nucleophile aims at the badge that attracts it and swaps out the halogen.
low.analogy: A magnet pair riveted into a chain link: the north-seeking nucleophile latches onto the exposed positive end and unhooks the negative neighbour.
low.examPointer: Write d+ on carbon and d- on halogen when sketching the mechanism - annotation is part of the drawn answer.

medium.restatement: The substitution conserves the carbon skeleton: one functional group leaves with the bonding pair, another arrives donating a pair. Charge flows from nucleophile through carbon to the departing halide.
medium.analogy: A relay race at the carbon atom: the incoming runner (nucleophile) hands electrons in, the outgoing runner (halide) carries the baton away.
medium.examPointer: Account for charges in every drawn step - a lone mechanism sketch without charge arrows loses method marks.

check.stem: In a nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane, the nucleophile attacks

options.text: The carbon atom carrying the partial positive charge
options.explanation: The d+ carbon is the electron-seeking target of the electron-rich nucleophile.

options.text: The halogen atom carrying the partial negative charge
options.explanation: Nucleophiles seek positive centres, not negative halogens.

options.text: A hydrogen atom on the chain
options.explanation: Attack lands at the functional carbon, not random hydrogens.

options.text: The solvent molecules
options.explanation: Solvent is not the substrate.

check.stem: Halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution because

options.text: The C-X bond is polar, giving carbon a partial positive charge
options.explanation: The d+ carbon invites electron-pair donation.

options.text: The C-X bond is non-polar and unstable
options.explanation: The bond is polar, not non-polar.

options.text: The halogen donates electrons to carbon
options.explanation: The halogen withdraws electron density; it does not donate.

options.text: Carbon repels the nucleophile
options.explanation: It attracts it.

check.stem: The species replaced by the nucleophile is

options.text: The halogen atom bearing the partial negative charge
options.explanation: X departs with the bond's electron pair as X-.

options.text: An alkyl group of the chain
options.explanation: The skeleton stays intact.

options.text: A hydrogen from the chain
options.explanation: No hydrogen leaves in substitution.

options.text: The solvent
options.explanation: Solvent is not part of the substrate.

check.stem: Which option correctly describes the electronic role of the nucleophile?

options.text: It donates a lone pair of electrons into the d+ carbon
options.explanation: Pair donation forms the new C-Nu bond.

options.text: It accepts an electron pair from carbon
options.explanation: That is electrophilic behaviour.

options.text: It removes a single electron, radical-style
options.explanation: No radical chemistry runs here.

options.text: It shares equally without net donation
options.explanation: Donation is directional and unequal.

check.stem: After the substitution, the halogen ends up as

options.text: A halide ion, X-, carrying the departed electron pair
options.explanation: Heterolytic departure hands both electrons to the halogen.

options.text: A neutral halogen molecule
options.explanation: No X2 forms in the substitution step.

options.text: A covalent acid HX
options.explanation: HX is not the immediate substitution product in alkali routes.

options.text: Still bonded to carbon
options.explanation: Substitution means it left.

check.stem: Define nucleophilic substitution.
check.modelAnswer: A reaction in which a nucleophile attacks a carbon with a partial positive charge and replaces the atom or group carrying the partial negative charge.

check.stem: State why the C-X bond is polar.
check.modelAnswer: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it draws the bonding electrons and carries the partial negative charge.

check.stem: Explain why the carbon of the C-X bond attracts nucleophiles.
check.modelAnswer: The electronegativity difference leaves carbon electron-poor (d+), and electron-rich nucleophiles are attracted to exactly such centres.

check.stem: Sketch reasoning: what happens to the electron pair of the C-X bond when the nucleophile attacks?
check.modelAnswer: The pair departs entirely with the halogen as X-, so the carbon never exceeds four bonds - the incoming nucleophile's pair replaces the departing one.

lessons.title: Mechanism with aqueous potassium hydroxide
lessons.opening: The hydroxide mechanism in full: lone pair out, C-O bond in, C-Br pair out with bromide. One concerted step, charges balanced, bromoethane into ethanol - the drawn answer every exam paper wants.
keyPoints: Mixed with aqueous alkali, the halogenoalkane converts into its alcohol by nucleophilic substitution.
The hydroxide ion donates its lone pair to the d+ carbon as the C-X pair departs with X-.
The one-step mechanism shows attack and departure simultaneously, with all charges shown.
Bromoethane plus OH- gives ethanol plus Br-.

low.restatement: OH- swings its lone pair onto carbon while the C-X electrons swing out to the halogen; one curved arrow out of OH-, one curved arrow onto X-, charges tracked throughout.
low.analogy: A revolving door at the carbon: OH- pushes in as Br- glides out, both moves drawn as one continuous turn.
low.examPointer: Draw both curly arrows (lone pair to carbon, C-X bond to X) and show the negative charges on OH- and X- - the full drawn mechanism is the mark scheme.

medium.restatement: The step is concerted: no intermediate forms, so the carbon never exceeds its four bonds. The nucleophile's donation and the leaving group's departure are electron-exact mirrors, conserving charge and atoms.
medium.analogy: A see-saw swapping riders at the carbon: one mounts as the other dismounts, and the board never wobbles beyond four bonds.
medium.examPointer: Check the charge ledger: reactant -1 (OH-) equals product -1 (Br-) after the neutral alcohol forms.

check.stem: In the OH- mechanism, the first curly arrow starts from

options.text: The lone pair on the hydroxide oxygen
options.explanation: The donation begins at the electron source - the OH- lone pair.

options.text: The carbon atom of the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Arrows show electron movement; carbon is the destination, not the source.

options.text: The halogen atom
options.explanation: The halogen's arrow runs in the opposite, departing direction.

options.text: The solvent
options.explanation: No solvent arrow appears in the step.

check.stem: The second curly arrow in the OH- mechanism shows

options.text: The C-X bonding pair moving onto the halogen atom
options.explanation: The departing pair lands on X, making X-.

options.text: The O-H bond pair moving to hydrogen
options.explanation: No O-H arrow exists in this step.

options.text: A hydrogen pair moving to oxygen
options.explanation: No hydrogen transfer occurs.

options.text: The C-C bond pair shifting
options.explanation: The skeleton stays intact.

check.stem: The overall charge ledger for CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br- shows

options.text: One negative charge on each side, carried by OH- then Br-
options.explanation: Neutral alcohol formation conserves the single negative unit.

options.text: Two negatives on the left and none on the right
options.explanation: Both sides carry exactly one negative charge.

options.text: Zero throughout
options.explanation: Ions are present on both sides.

options.text: A positive charge appearing mid-mechanism
options.explanation: No positive intermediate forms in the concerted step.

check.stem: Why does no intermediate form in the OH- substitution mechanism?

options.text: Attack and departure happen in one concerted step
options.explanation: The entering and exiting movements are simultaneous.

options.text: The carbon rejects any fifth bond
options.explanation: That is the consequence, not the step's classification.

options.text: The solvent blocks intermediates
options.explanation: Solvent does not forbid intermediates.

options.text: Bromide is too slow to leave
options.explanation: It leaves exactly as OH- arrives.

check.stem: The product alcohol in the aqueous alkali mechanism forms because

options.text: The carbon-oxygen bond replaces the carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: The OH group stays covalently attached to the carbon skeleton.

options.text: The hydroxide remains an ion in solution
options.explanation: It is consumed into the neutral alcohol.

options.text: The halogen donates electrons to oxygen
options.explanation: No such donation occurs.

options.text: Water adds across the chain
options.explanation: No addition chemistry runs in substitution.

check.stem: Write the overall equation for bromoethane with aqueous OH-.
check.modelAnswer: CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br-, the alcohol and bromide ion.

check.stem: State the two curly arrows drawn in the OH- mechanism.
check.modelAnswer: One from the OH- lone pair to the d+ carbon, one from the C-X bond onto the halogen as X- leaves.

check.stem: Explain why the mechanism is described as substitution.
check.modelAnswer: One group (OH) substitutes into the position vacated by another (Br), on an unchanged carbon skeleton - the defining pattern of substitution.

check.stem: A student draws the OH- mechanism but forgets the negative charge on the departing bromide. Why is the drawing wrong?
check.modelAnswer: The C-X bonding pair departs WITH the halogen, so bromide must carry the negative charge - omitting it breaks both the charge ledger and the electron bookkeeping.

lessons.title: Mechanism with ammonia: the two-step to amines
lessons.opening: Ammonia's substitution runs in two beats: the lone pair lands on carbon making a charged salt, then a second ammonia deprotonates it. Chloromethane to methylamine with ammonium chloride as the co-product shows both steps.
keyPoints: Ammonia reacts with a halogenoalkane by nucleophilic substitution in two steps.
Step 1: CH3Cl + NH3 -> [CH3NH3]+Cl-, forming the substituted ammonium salt.
Step 2: [CH3NH3]+Cl- + NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl, deprotonation by a second ammonia.
Excess ammonia favours the primary amine over further substitution.

low.restatement: Beat one installs NH3 on carbon (nitrogen now bears four bonds and a positive charge); beat two's ammonia removes the extra proton, leaving the neutral primary amine and NH4Cl.
low.analogy: A guest (NH3) moves in with an extra suitcase (proton); a second guest takes the suitcase away, leaving a tidy resident (NH2).
low.examPointer: Draw step 1's arrow from the N lone pair to carbon and step 2's from the second NH3 lone pair to an N-H hydrogen - both arrows are examinable.

medium.restatement: The intermediate [CH3NH3]+ is a substituted ammonium ion; its deprotonation is a simple acid-base step where ammonia acts as base. The chloride ion pairs with NH4+ as the inorganic co-product.
medium.analogy: The intermediate is a four-legged nitrogen stool: one leg (proton) is borrowed by the second ammonia, restoring the three-legged amine.
medium.examPointer: Name the co-product ammonium chloride and mark the charge balance across both steps.

check.stem: The intermediate in the ammonia mechanism is

options.text: [CH3NH3]+Cl-, a substituted ammonium salt
options.explanation: Nitrogen carries four bonds and the positive charge after attack.

options.text: CH3NH2 free amine
options.explanation: That is the final product, after deprotonation.

options.text: CH3NH2+ radical
options.explanation: No radicals form.

options.text: NH4OH
options.explanation: No such intermediate appears.

check.stem: The role of the second ammonia molecule is

options.text: To remove a proton from the intermediate, forming NH4Cl and the free amine
options.explanation: Ammonia acts as base in the deprotonation beat.

options.text: To attack carbon a second time
options.explanation: The carbon already carries its nitrogen.

options.text: To replace the chloride ion
options.explanation: Chloride simply pairs with NH4+.

options.text: To catalyse the first step
options.explanation: Each ammonia is consumed stoichiometrically.

check.stem: In the first beat, where does the attacking lone pair of ammonia land?

options.text: The lone pair on ammonia's nitrogen to the d+ carbon
options.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair is the electron source.

options.text: The C-Cl bond to the carbon
options.explanation: The C-Cl pair departs to chlorine instead.

options.text: Chloride to nitrogen
options.explanation: Chloride is a spectator until pairing with NH4+.

options.text: A C-H bond to nitrogen
options.explanation: No C-H arrow exists here.

check.stem: The co-product NH4Cl forms in step 2 because

options.text: The second ammonia keeps the removed proton, pairing with chloride
options.explanation: NH3 + H+ -> NH4+ alongside the existing Cl-.

options.text: Chloride attacks ammonia
options.explanation: Chloride has no attacking role.

options.text: Ammonia decomposes to nitrogen and hydrogen
options.explanation: No decomposition occurs.

options.text: The solvent supplies the proton
options.explanation: The proton comes from the intermediate's nitrogen.

check.stem: Excess ammonia is used in this route to

options.text: Prevent the amine product reacting further by substitution
options.explanation: Surplus NH3 out-competes the amine as nucleophile.

options.text: Speed up the deprotonation step only
options.explanation: The excess also guards against over-substitution.

options.text: Dissolve the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Ethanol is the solvent.

options.text: Neutralise the ammonium chloride
options.explanation: No neutralisation is intended.

check.stem: Write the two equations for chloromethane with ammonia.
check.modelAnswer: CH3Cl + NH3 -> [CH3NH3]+Cl-; then [CH3NH3]+Cl- + NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl.

check.stem: Name the final organic product and the inorganic co-product.
check.modelAnswer: The primary amine (e.g. methylamine) and ammonium chloride.

check.stem: Explain why the intermediate carries a positive charge on nitrogen.
check.modelAnswer: After donating its lone pair, nitrogen holds four bonds (three H plus the carbon) and thus one unit of formal positive charge.

check.stem: Sum the two ammonia steps into one overall equation for chloromethane.
check.modelAnswer: CH3Cl + 2NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl: one ammonia attacks, the second deprotonates, so two equivalents are consumed overall.

glossary.definition: The reaction class in which an electron-pair donor replaces an atom or group on an electron-poor carbon.
The departing species (here the halide ion) that takes the bonding electron pair with it.
The positive intermediate formed when ammonia's nitrogen bonds to carbon, before deprotonation.

workedExample.prompt: Combine the two ammonia mechanism steps for chloromethane into one overall equation, checking the atom and charge ledgers.
steps: Step 1: CH3Cl + NH3 -> [CH3NH3]+Cl- (nitrogen attacks, chloride departs with the pair).
Step 2: [CH3NH3]+Cl- + NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl (second ammonia removes the spare proton).
Cancel the intermediate [CH3NH3]+Cl- appearing on both sides of the summed equation.
Check the ledger: carbons 1 = 1, hydrogens 3+3+3 = 5+4 = 9, nitrogens 1+1 = 1+1, chlorines 1 = 1, total charge 0 = 0.
